text.p: Connecticut's Supreme Court ruled Monday that the state's law requiring safe storage of guns at home was constitutional.

The ruling came in the case of Joseph Wilchinski of Glastonbury, Connecticut, whose teenage son accidentally shot a friend to death with Wilchinski's pistol in 1993, Chief State's Attorney John Bailey said.
The son removed the unsecured handgun from a zippered case, underneath a dresser.
The youth was not charged, but Wilchinski was charged with negligent storage of a firearm, and sentenced to probation.
Wilchinski appealed, arguing the law was vague.
The 1990 law, known as the "kids and guns" bill, was enacted in response to growing concern over accidental shootings of children.
"Today's decision is important because the law it upholds is important to the protection of children, who all too often are the unintended targets of accidental gun shots," Bailey said.

"The court's decision leaves no doubt that the 'kids and guns' bill means just what it says -- if you have a loaded firearm under your control you must safeguard that weapon against use by children and, if you fail to do so, and someone is hurt or killed, you will be prosecuted for a felony."
